stories.title: Health risks and lag effects of ambient PM2.5 exposure on respiratory and cardiovascular mortality and morbidity in Ratchaburi, Thailand
stories.description: Exposure to ambient PM2.5 is a well-established environmental risk factor associated with adverse respiratory and cardiovascular health outcomes. Ratchaburi, Thailand, has experienced increasing concerns regarding ambient PM2.5 pollution. This study investigated the associations between ambient PM2.5 exposure and respiratory and cardiovascular mortality and morbidity in Ratchaburi from 2015 to 2019 using a distributed lag non-linear model (DLNM). The exposure–lag–response relationships were assessed on the current day of exposure and up to seven days following exposure. For all ages and all genders, a 10 µg/m³ increase in PM2.5 was associated with a 5.42% (95% CI 1.85–9.12%) increase in respiratory mortality at lag0, and a 2.69% (95% CI 1.45–3.95%) increase in respiratory morbidity at lag0-6. Cardiovascular mortality increased by 3.55% (95% CI 0.23–6.99%) at lag0-5 and cardiovascular morbidity by 1.85% (95% CI − 0.24–3.98%) at lag0-6. The observed associations varied across age and gender categories. Elderly individuals generally showed higher risks for respiratory mortality, while adults showed higher risks for respiratory morbidity and cardiovascular mortality. Females generally showed higher associations for respiratory and cardiovascular morbidity, whereas males showed higher associations for cardiovascular mortality. Overall, the findings provide local epidemiological evidence regarding short-term PM2.5 exposure and associated respiratory and cardiovascular health burdens in Ratchaburi, Thailand. The observed exposure–lag–response relationships support future public health planning and air quality management strategies related to PM2.5 exposure in areas experiencing elevated PM2.5 concentrations.

stories.title: Combined effects of 450, 635 and 980 nm LASER wavelengths on proliferation and migration of human periodontal ligament mesenchymal stem cells
stories.description: This in vitro investigation was conducted to compare the efficacy of various wavelengths individually [450 nm (G1), 635 nm (G2), 980 nm (G3)] or in combination [450 nm + 635 nm (G4); 450 nm + 980 nm (G5); 635 nm + 980 nm (G6); and 450 nm + 635 nm + 980 nm (G7)] on cellular viability, proliferation, and migration of human periodontal ligament stem cells (hPDLSCs). In combined-wavelengths groups (G4, G5, G6, G7), laser irradiation was performed simultaneously through a single probe. All groups received 10 uninterrupted seconds of irradiation with each wavelengths set at 4 J/cm2 energy density and 200 mW power. MTT assay, DAPI staining, scratch migration assay, Ki67 marker expression, Annexin V/PI assay (apoptosis), and proliferatory/migratory factors through ELISA (SDF-1, VEGF and TGF-β1) were utilized from 1 to 6 days post-irradiation. All groups were compared against each-other and a control negative (no laser therapy) group. The statistical analysis was evaluated using Two-way ANOVA (P < 0.05). MTT and DAPI assays showed significantly higher metabolic activity/viability rates for G1, G5 and G7. The expression rate of Ki67 and its mean fluorescent intensity were both superior in G7. G7 had the most stable outcomes in apoptosis tests. hPDLSCs had the greatest migratory capability in G6 and G7 in the first 2 days. The highest concentrations of SDF-1, VEGF and TGF- β1 were observed in G1, G5 and G7, respectively. It is worth noting that combined-wavelength groups had overall higher energy densities and powers than individual-wavelength groups. Given the outstanding proliferative and migrative outcomes of blue light (450 nm) individually or in combination with red and near-infrared wavelengths on hPDLSCs, further studies must incorporate blue light lasers in photobiomodulation therapy. All wavelengths were set at 4 J/cm2; further dose-matched studies must be conducted to reach firm conclusions.

stories.title: Threshold-free neural network models for swim bout detection of larval zebrafish
stories.description: Accurate detection of swim bouts is essential for decoding motor behavior in larval zebrafish, yet conventional threshold-based methods rely on subjective cutoffs and per-experiment tuning. To address this limitation, we developed threshold-free deep learning models operating on tail-curvature time series: an offline model for post hoc analysis and an online model for real-time detection. Both improved precision over threshold-based methods, particularly for low-amplitude bouts. Using the offline model, we show that a head-fixed, closed-loop preparation largely preserves naturalistic swimming kinematics. Repeated trials reduced bout frequency and increased interbout interval, whereas genetic background primarily affects bout duration and maximum amplitude; notably, casper larvae lacked the late-trial decline observed in wildtype and nacre. We further show that detector choice can alter inferred behavioral outcomes. Together, these results establish a high-throughput framework for robust and reproducible analysis of zebrafish swimming behavior across experimental conditions.
